Some parts of the edd.load module were using lists as parameters, derived from

Add overhauled import workflow

We have a need to update several parts of the data ingestion solutions
available in EDD, and in particular adding support for setting metadata with
data, during one import file upload. There is also a need to boost performance,
particularly around bulk database inserts.

The existing APIs for these features are too rigid to allow for comfortable
modifications. The `reader` module is an attempt to refresh the APIs, to do the
same functionality while allowing for the new features to be added as well. The
module contains replacements for much of the code in the
`edd.load.parsers.core` module. A main focus is to simplify the APIs and to
support iteration and incremental updates as much as possible.

All frontend code is replaced. Where the existing frontend is the only piece of
EDD making use of React, and works as a single-page app embedded in EDD and
interacts with custom REST APIs, the new frontend uses traditional HTML forms
and minimal JavaScript. The little JavaScript it includes is mainly to
facilitate inline updates of progress bars--the primary "new" feature of the
frontend. Otherwise, the layout and functionality is purposefully mimicing the
existing frontend, with minor updates for a11y and to switch to Bootstrap 5.

This is a __*LOT*__ of code removed. All the React front-end is gone. Most of
the custom and flaky error reporting framework is ripped out; the custom
Exception attributes are kept in place, but the rest is removed. We can adapt
these later to more standard error reporting. A lot of the database models are
no longer needed. The REST API subsystem for imports is gone. All the resolving
code that relied on loading the entire import in memory is gone, in favor of
the newer generator/iterator based resolving. The clone of the notification
system specific to the React front-end is gone, in favor of the simpler
progress bar update websocket.

Fix attach of click handler to permission button

This was a long-standing annoying bug on Firefox, but worked fine on Chrome and
Safari until very recently. It appears that setting the click handler on the
permission button was failing, because the function that added the handler was
wrapped in a page load event handler, which in turn was wrapped in a handler
that waited for the EDD AJAX data for the study to download. The page would
finish loading before the AJAX custom event fired, and thus the handler that
attached the click event would not run.

From a quick scan, it appears there is no longer any code in the setup for
permissions that requires waiting for the AJAX payload to finish downloading
and processing. Moving the permission setup to the top level of the script,
next to the custom event, fixes the problem. It seems that Firefox was first to
stop processing handlers for a load event if the event handler is registered
*after* the page already loaded. Chrome and Safari were continuing to
automatically trigger the handler if the page already loaded until recently.

Use container static files as default fallback

Building the EDD image will bundle in static assets with the Docker image. When
running in development with volume-mounted code, there will often not be any
static assets saved in the working development directory. This is causing a
fresh clone and startup to fail, as EDD will try to read static assets from the
volume-mounted directory, and nothing will be there in a fresh clone. Setting
the bundled version as an additional location with STATICFILES_DIRS will allow
those files to be found, and for startup to complete.

Fix color selection when filtering out-of-order

When filtering lines in the graph view out-of-order, the color assignment was
happening in the order of items in the filter list, but any items already
having an assigned color would keep that color. Because of this, any lines that
were already selected could get their colors prematurely assigned to earlier
items in the list. Instead, doing one pass to find items missing a color
assignment, then a second pass to do the actual assignment of the next
available color.

Eliminate test errors dependent on execution order

Some tests were throwing errors depending on the order of test execution. Two
such errors are corrected here. First, several places in EDD code make use of
a threadlocal variable for the current request; a custom TestCase class that
clears this threadlocal variable during class and test setUp/tearDown was in
the main.tests module, and is now copied to the edd module. Second, some code
in the edd_utils module was using delayed imports; this delayed import could
result in a SciPy module loading that tries to iterate over globals(), but
the act of importing modifies globals() and results in a RuntimeError in
Python3.6 because the globals() dictionary is modified during iteration. By
moving the imports back to top-level and not delaying, the error is avoided.

Upgrade JQuery type definitions to 3.x

We've been using JQuery version 3.x for some time, but were still on the 2.x
type definitions. The biggest difference is the 3.x definitions are much more
explicit about the return value of jQuery().val(); where before the definitions
essentially returned `any`, now it specifies `string | number | string[]`, as
technically a `<select multiple="multiple">` input type can return an array of
strings. The docs also mention the possibility of returning a number, but this
does not appear to happen (even with `<input type="number">`). So now the code
must do `$(selector).val() as string` to make it explicit that we're not
dealing with a multiple select.

Pinning this to 3.3.35, because 3.3.36 introduces a regression where some
JQuery methods end up getting type mismatches between JQuery<Element> and
JQuery<HTMLElement>.

Upgrade to Django 5.0.x releases

Cleanup a handful of DeprecationWarnings that either already existed in EDD or
were triggered by an upgrade of Django to 5.0 from the previous bound of <4.2.

The Solr code was making use of `datetime.datetime.utcnow()`, which has been
deprecated for some time. The function returns a `datetime` with the current
UTC time, however, it returns it as a *naïve* `datetime`, without the `tzinfo`
timezone attribute set. This can cause issues, as Python defaults to treating
naïve `datetime` objects as in the system locale timezone. It's not impactful
in EDD's code, but regardless, the call is updated to use `arrow`'s functions
which will explicitly attach the UTC timezone to the object.

Some admin views would directly render an `Update` model to a string, and the
`__str__` method of the model uses the `arrow` library `humanize` method. This
would also make use of `datetime.datetime.utcnow()`, *unless* you explicitly
pass a time to compare. So, explicitly adding a non-deprecated comparison time.

The `edd.branding` module made use of Django's `django.utils.html.format_html`
function, which now warns if not passing an `args` or `kwargs` to fill
placeholders in the format string. EDD was doing this everywhere except for
default fallback values, using the empty string. These fallback values don't
need passing to `format_html`, can can simply return the empty string.

Django's default for URLs submitted in forms with `django.forms.URLField` is
changing from assuming an "http" scheme to assuming "https", and emits a
warning if a field is using the assumed scheme. There's a global setting for
this, added to EDD's base settings. The global setting itself is deprecated, as
it will be removed in Django 6.0; when upgrading to Django 6.0, the setting and
its warning filter should be removed.

See: https://blog.ganssle.io/articles/2019/11/utcnow.html
See: https://adamj.eu/tech/2023/12/07/django-fix-urlfield-assume-scheme-warnings/

Update http service to use Gunicorn+uvicorn

In some testing I've done in local development in changing the proxy to EDD
services has revealed that ASGI server(s) like Daphne and Gunicorn run with a
uvicorn worker, are capable of handling both HTTP and WebSocket traffic. This
update switches the "main" `http` service to run Gunicorn with a uvicorn
worker. Originally, I tried with only Daphne, but it does not have as much
production-hardening, and doesn't support code reload with a hangup signal.

Once this is deployed to production, configs can be changed to only have two
containers using the EDD image, one for handling both HTTP and WebSocket
traffic, and the other to run Celery for background workers. The existing
`websocket` service can be removed, and the complicated proxy setup splitting
traffic between the two services can revert to a simple proxy.

After some time, we can also remove the Daphne dependency, and likely a few
others that were used by Daphne (gevent?).

Fix attach of click handler to permission button

This was a long-standing annoying bug on Firefox, but worked fine on Chrome and
Safari until very recently. It appears that setting the click handler on the
permission button was failing, because the function that added the handler was
wrapped in a page load event handler, which in turn was wrapped in a handler
that waited for the EDD AJAX data for the study to download. The page would
finish loading before the AJAX custom event fired, and thus the handler that
attached the click event would not run.

From a quick scan, it appears there is no longer any code in the setup for
permissions that requires waiting for the AJAX payload to finish downloading
and processing. Moving the permission setup to the top level of the script,
next to the custom event, fixes the problem. It seems that Firefox was first to
stop processing handlers for a load event if the event handler is registered
*after* the page already loaded. Chrome and Safari were continuing to
automatically trigger the handler if the page already loaded until recently.

Fix import statements to reference true dependency

Several parts of the edd_file_importer tests were importing dependencies by
depending on the dependencies of unrelated modules. Replacing these transitive
dependencies with imports to the actual dependency source, instead.

As an example, if you have modules A.py and B.py, both depending on code in
module C.py as below, then the correct way for both A and B to import is from
C, not from each other.

    # C.py
    def shared_dependency():
        pass

    # A.py
    # this is the way
    from .C import shared_dependency

    # B.py
    # should not do this!
    from .A import shared_dependency

It is a bad practice to use this transitive dependency importing, because by
doing so, the implementation of e.g. module B becomes more tightly coupled to
the implementation of module A. Should module A update in the future to no
longer depend on C.shared_dependency, then module B will break!

Adding a Lines-only disambiguation mode, to disambiguate Lines without also disambiguating Assays, allowing for the creation of matrices of new Lines/Assays.

Example:
Set 1: Line: Fred, Assay: Bob, Measurement: Glucose
Set 2: Line: Bill, Assay: Bob, Measurement: Glucose
Set 3: Line: Fred, Assay: Joe, Measurement: Glucose
Set 4: Line: Bill, Assay: Joe, Measurement: Glucose

In the original disambiguation mode, the user would only be able to disambiguate against the Assay.  So Assay "Bob" would be connected to a single unique Assay, and Assay "Joe" would be connected to another, and the contents of "Line" would be disregarded.  Set 2 would overwrite Set 1, and Set 4 would overwrite Set 3.

In the new Lines-only mode, the user would connect "Fred" and "Bill" with one Line each, and "Bob" and "Joe" would become new Assays under each.  Four Assays under two Lines would be created in total, each with a separate Glucose measurement.

The new mode is currently used only for the Biolector imports.

Fix login failure when Solr is unresponsive

Adding a try-catch and logging a warning whenever the code updating the Solr
indices fails.

the last login time set to the current time. When the database record updates,
that triggers an update to Solr. But, if Solr is unresponsive or down, the
index update will throw an exception. If that exception is not caught, it
bubbles up until it ultimately fails the login request.

Fix deleting of lines

Django as of 3.2 dis-allows doing QuerySet .delete() calls after calls to
.distinct(), because in some cases there are reports of .delete() after
.distinct() generating SQL like `DELETE FROM table;`. Deletion of lines is
making use of the ExportSelection class, that can take identifiers for studies,
lines, assays, and measurements, and create a selection that includes all
parent objects for the given identifiers, and all child objects. This ends up
using a call to .distinct() for each level. Getting around the limitation by
selecting the id values for lines, then doing a delete on lines having id in
that set.

Fix auto-validation of emails from LDAP

The LDAP backend code has a hook so that any email address coming from LDAP
gets auto-verified, so that users do not need to receive an email and click on
a verification link. This code was using update_or_create() to add an entry in
the database for the email, but because it was using a filter of email__iexact,
it would end up always trying to insert an empty email address. The
documentation on update_or_create() points to get_or_create() to describe how
filters are handled, and the algorithm described excludes any filters that are
not direct fields. The change here modifies the validation hook to properly set
the email from LDAP, and cleans up edge-cases.

Replace patched cleanse_setting with new API

Django prior to 3.2 used a function `django.views.debug.cleanse_setting()` to
replace any potentially sensitive parameters in settings with an obfuscated
value (a string of asterisks). In Django 3.2+, this function is replaced by a
SafeExceptionReporterFilter class, that handles cleansing settings, as well as
sensitive parameters in request META headers and post parameters, when
reporting values in errors.

EDD was using a monkey-patched version of `cleanse_setting`, that checked for
keys likely to contain URLs, then parse those URLs and replace any found
passwords with asterisks. Now that the original function is gone and refactored
into a class swappable in settings, moved the patched code into a sub-class of
the new class, and changed the base EDD settings to load our version of
the class.

Update Django i18n templatetag names

The canonical names for the Django translation templatetags are updated,
switching from `trans` to `translate`, and `blocktrans` / `endblocktrans` to
`blocktranslate` / `endblocktranslate`. The prior names will still function,
but are no longer documented. Updating our uses of these templatetags to use
the un-abbreviated and more explicit new canonical names.

Did this with two commands:

    find . -type f -path '*/templates/*' -exec sed -i "" -E 's/blocktrans /blocktranslate /g' {} \;
    find . -type f -path '*/templates/*' -exec sed -i "" -E 's/{% trans /{% translate /g' {} \;

Further fixes for lint errors re: missing type information on the public
interfaces for modules. Fixes here are all for React-related code used in the
import wizard.

Note: there will still show some errors when directly using the `tsc` compiler.
Our normal builds go through webpack, with the `ts-loader` plugin. The loader
does the correct thing for code like: `import * from "./MyModule.tsx";`. While
using the compiler directly will complain, because TypeScript wants all
extensions removed from imports. The code will not function if the extensions
are left off, so any editors that attempt to highlight errors will mark these
imports as broken. There is an open issue with the TypeScript development team,
which will allow for explicit extensions in imports. It's unlikely to get done
anytime soon. Therefore: trust the build script above any errors reported via
your editor of choice.

records, the methods are changed to use just the array of records. Client code

generating the JQuery object for those records.

Fix line editing when a strain value is present

Jennifer reported a bug where she was unable to edit line names in EDD. After
further investigation, I found that the bug was not with editing line names,
but doing any edits on lines containing strain links.

There are a few interacting bugs at play. One that delayed diagnosis of the
root cause is a bug where the strain autocomplete from ICE was sending EDD the
ICE database primary key value, where it should have sent the strain UUID. This
is updated now to return the correct values. There remains a TODO for a future
enhancement, to make use of the additional data ICE makes available on search
results, so EDD can display more than just the entry name in ICE.

The true root cause of the errors hit by Jennifer have to do with the order of
operations Django is using to validate values to a ModelChoiceField. We have a
RegistryValidator class that will auto-create EDD Strain model entries from an
ICE entry; but this only runs after the Django ModelChoiceField does its
validations. So we're stuck in a spot where we can't validate a UUID matches
an ICE strain until we have a saved model instance, and we can't have a saved
model instance until we validate a UUID matches an ICE strain.

After some experimentation, I settled on making a custom Field class, which
extends ModelMultipleChoiceField, and ensure that the translation of values
from a form submit to the values validated by the Field first run through
RegistryValidator. This fixes the order of operations, so we check ICE first,
creating an EDD model instance if needed, then do foreign key database ops.

Replace Django CharField with custom VarCharField

The default Django models CharField requires use of a max_length argument,
resulting in a database column of `varchar(n)`. This runs counter to
recommendations from Postgres, which says to use just `varchar`, and set any
needed constraints with check constraints. Here I am changing all the
django.db.models.CharField instances on models to a new edd.fields.VarCharField
model. I am also retroactively renaming an older
main.models.fields.VarCharField to its new location.

See https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Don't_Do_This for more details.

Fix email notification on account enable

When an admin user approves accounts, an email should go out to the user with
the approved account. If this is done individually on each profile page, it
works; if it's done from the list and the action dropdown, it was broken. The
action would do an `update()` on a queryset, then would loop the *same*
queryset to send emails; however, the `update()` and the loop both re-evaluate
the queryset, in a way where the loop would always be an empty queryset.
Forcing the queryset into a `list` before doing the `update` allows for
scheduling the email task for all the users affected.

Remove multiprocessing from init-config invoke

Following the addition of some debugging code to the EDD config container
invoke script in commit fe6f8db5be97a806ef9004dd953d10f0d066253b, I finally
caught some clues to why Jenkins will sometimes fail builds in the init step.
Now that it's printing some progress information, Jenkins can show more closely
where the process is failing. The output on the failed run was:

    Configuring postgres
    Configuring rabbitmq
    Configuring redis
    Configuring mail
    Configuring solr
    Configuring nginx
    Configuring ice
    Configuring core
      yq w -s /tmp/http.script -i service/http.yml
      yq w -s /tmp/websocket.script -i service/websocket.yml
      yq w -s /tmp/worker.script -i service/worker.yml
      yq w -s /tmp/postgres.script -i service/postgres.yml
      yq w -s /tmp/rabbitmq.script -i service/rabbitmq.yml
      yq w -s /tmp/ice.script -i service/ice.yml

The lines reading "Configuring ..." are prints, and the "yq" lines are shell
commands executed by the config invoke script. The script was building a list
of individual services to configure, then was running them in subprocesses
using multiprocessing.Pool. It looks like the problem is the Pool object is
using map, but will sometimes fail to block until all the items passed into
map() finish processing. There should be lines like the following once all the
yq scripts are run, but they are missing:

      yq m -a service/http.yml service/websocket.yml service/worker.yml \
          service/postgres.yml service/rabbitmq.yml service/ice.yml \
          service/smtp.yml service/redis.yml service/solr.yml \
          > /tmp/edd-config/docker-compose.override.yml
      tar -czf /tmp/edd-config.tgz -C /tmp/edd-config .

The multiprocessing module was included originally because of large amounts of
latency when running the script, in an attempt to divide-and-conquer the work.
The latency turned out to be because passing data to a shell subprocess
standard input directly, would write to the shell command one byte at a time,
with a sleep between each byte. Rather than trying to access standard input,
all subshells are instead writing out data to temporary files, and passing the
temporary file in the subshell command. With the latency gone, there's no
longer a need for multiprocessing, and it's apparently causing a problem. So
now, it's gone.

Use container static files as default fallback

Building the EDD image will bundle in static assets with the Docker image. When
running in development with volume-mounted code, there will often not be any
static assets saved in the working development directory. This is causing a
fresh clone and startup to fail, as EDD will try to read static assets from the
volume-mounted directory, and nothing will be there in a fresh clone. Setting
the bundled version as an additional location with STATICFILES_DIRS will allow
those files to be found, and for startup to complete.

EDD to work correctly from a fresh clone as described in the documentation.

assign real host strings to the ALLOWED_HOSTS setting.

Update tests to clean up uploaded attachments

The test suite has a few tests that upload attachments as part of the test.
These files would get written to the storage backend configured for the
environment, and could pile up over time. These tests should now be fixed to
clean up after themselves, so there won't be several copies of the same fixture
files duplicated every time a dev environment runs tests.

Part of the update is changing how attachments are handled. They now will
special-case attachments created by the `system` user (typically only from
migrations / bootstrapping code), and store these at the media root. Normal
attachments go into directories for the current date as before, but are now
also prefixed with the parent object ID. This will prevent potential issues
where two users upload a file with the same name, on the same day, but with
different content. With how the code was working, this would result in the
second uploaded file overwriting the first. Now, both will get unique names
based on where the attachment is added. One caveat, if a file is uploaded to
the same study, with the same name, on the same day, the same behavior will
occur. This is obscure enough to not worry about unless / until someone
triggers it and complains.

In some exports, including worklists, there would be excessive log output
because of inadequate filtering of values before rendering. Specifically, if an
export is selected with a column for strain information, on a Study with one or
more Line objects without strains, then a TypeError would get logged because of
converting a `[None]` to a pipe-delimited string of names. There is a similar
problem in worklists, where the renderer is making use of the `to_json()`
function on `EDDObject`, which tries to render full update objects to JSON; but
the `created`/`updated` fields may not be included in the query
`select_related()`, and the render would fail.

In both these cases, the exports would work fine, there would just be a lot of
log output. The excessive output makes it harder to filter down to
actual problems.

Fix some overlooked template items

As I was working on #1323, I found / re-discovered a potential gotcha in
templates, in dealing with the `blocktranslate` tags. While in most other parts
of templates using Django's templating language, items enclosed in double curly
brackets `{{}}` can have "filters" applied, text inside a `blocktranslate`
treats the text inside the brackets as a literal key to the template context.
The result will generally be a key not found in the context, and the variable
"expands" to an empty string. In the case of my re-discovery, this was in the
form of trying to do `{{ site_name|default:"EDD" }}`, so the site name would
print, and "EDD" would print if the name wasn't set. What really happens is
that instead of looking up a variable `site_name`, the template tries to look
up a variable `site_name|default:"EDD"` and yields the empty string (because
*of course* that "variable" doesn't exist).

While searching through templates for other potential cases of this error, I
also did a quick search on the `load` template tag, and where there were
multiples of these, consolidated into a single tag. For example `{% load i18n
%}{% load static %}` can be simply `{% load i18n static %}`.

    Which is a command that will do all processing up-to-and-including running
    Django migrations, then stop.

    Another feature enabled by `invoke` is the ability to use the same Python code
    as the rest of EDD to load external services. This means that the Compose file
    can consist of only container definitions for the http, websocket, and task
    workers, and `postgres`, `rabbitmq`, `redis`, `smtp`, and `solr` are all
    optional, as long as some URL is available for each service during startup.
    This also means there no longer needs to be one "blessed" container responsible
    for startup tasks on shared resources. Any container can execute these checks,
    at any time, and may scale up beyond 1 container.

Add Django DEFAULT_AUTO_FIELD setting

With Django 3.2, the auto-generated primary key field on models is
configurable. The previous default would use an IntegerField (32-bit) under the
hood, while the new default uses a BigIntegerField (64-bit). With this switch,
there are now migration warnings. Explicitly adding a value of AutoField uses
the old behavior, and does not result in a whole-database migration.

Improve build process for edd-core Dockerfile

building. The result of these tweaks are a final image that's about 40MB

Adding an additional build argument, `REPO_SERVER`, for specifying which
container registry to use for base images. The default is set to "docker.io",
which is the same as just leaving it blank. This will let our automated builds
specify our local registry instead during builds, to avoid needing to pull or

The build phases are now more strictly separating the TypeScript builds from
the Python code. There should no longer be a need to wait for TypeScript to
rebuild if only Python code is changing, which will save significant time;
TypeScript builds typically take over a minute. An additional build phase is
added to load in the current git commit hash, which was previously being done
along with the TypeScript build. The Python code is now loaded in directly,
instead of being passed along from the TypeScript build phase. This means that
Python-only changes can now be rebuilt in a matter of seconds.

    Some tests were throwing errors depending on the order of test execution. Two
    such errors are corrected here. First, several places in EDD code make use of
    a threadlocal variable for the current request; a custom TestCase class that
    clears this threadlocal variable during class and test setUp/tearDown was in
    the main.tests module, and is now copied to the edd module. Second, some code
    in the edd_utils module was using delayed imports; this delayed import could
    result in a SciPy module loading that tries to iterate over globals(), but
    the act of importing modifies globals() and results in a RuntimeError in
    Python3.6 because the globals() dictionary is modified during iteration. By
    moving the imports back to top-level and not delaying, the error is avoided.

Change to custom user model

Replacing the monkey-patched functions on the User object with a real custom
User class that extends the default Django AbstractUser class. This makes the
application setup slightly simpler, because we don't need to hook in to add the
monkey-patched functions at the right time anymore; and Django will no longer
detect pending migrations for the django.contrib.auth app anymore because of
our custom Manager object that fetches the Profile associated with a user.

Changes here are roughly following the outline given in:
https://www.caktusgroup.com/blog/2019/04/26/how-switch-custom-django-user-model-mid-project/
and
https://code.djangoproject.com/ticket/25313

Since we don't care much about the table name in the database, using the same
auto-generated name in the standard Django model is fine. Since we also have a
freshly-squashed migration in the edd.profile app, and that app also deals with
User-related things, adding in the definition for the new User model there
allows for everything to continue functioning exactly as before for existing
installations, and still work for brand-new installations.

Remove Phosphor measurement type

The commonly-used measurement types in EDD right now are:
- "Generic", measurements without any specific external references or other
  metadata, e.g. "OD600", "pH"
- "Metabolite", measurements of small molecules, almost all of which have a
  reference to PubChem
- "ProteinIdentifier", measurements of peptides, almost all of which have a
  reference to UniProt or ICE
- "GeneIdentifier", measurements of RNA transcripts; these mostly *don't* have
  external references, though the plan is to support NCBI and/or ICE

There's also one other measurement type, "Phosphor", which was meant to be a
measurement of specific light wavelengths from phosphorescence / fluorescence /
luminescence. It was only ever used once, for the Reider Apel et al paper using
the flow cytometer to characterize promoter expression levels. The idea was we
would eventually get the analysis pipeline from Jake Beal to better quantize
signals from the flow cytometer, and it would be good to have measurement types
that referenced the analysis, had metadata on excitation and emission
wavelengths, etc. But, this never happened. And we have a bunch of code that is
essentially unused beyond the basics of code shared between all types.

In the interest in keeping the code simple, migrate the few entries that are
using this measurement type to a generic measurement, then delete the tables
and code for "Phosphor". If we ever get back into seriously supporting the flow
cytometer, it can do the same thing with generic measurement types; and if
there's an external datasource / ontology we want to reference, we can revisit
adding back something that will explicitly reference that external source like
the other 'omics types.

Add a display name field to user profiles

This change adds a field to every user's Profile for a display name. This is
overall good practice to have, given reasons listed in "Falsehoods Programmers
Believe About Names" ([link][names]), and that Django's defaults violate this
by having `first_name` and `last_name` fields. Adding a field for this allows
for a consistent and *updatable* bit of text to use to refer to a specific
person or account.

Additionally, adding this field enables an easier implementation of a nifty
feature, where a single autocomplete field can be used to select a user *or*
group for things like setting permissions. With a properly constructed UNION
query, we can search through both kinds of records and deal with the response
records in a single query. Without it, two different queries would need to
happen, then merge the results, then order the merged results in application
code … and it's a huge mess. Implementing convoluted logic to "compute" this
value for users from multiple different fields is prone to error, as well.

Add support for using S3 storage backend

This is a necessary step for moving toward multiple-node setups of EDD, where
we cannot guarantee that nodes will have access to the same filesystem. Using
NFS for sharing a filesystem does not play well with Django, as it makes use of
filesystem locking. Locking through the filesystem is fraught enough, and doing
so over NFS only compounds the problem. Using a storage backend with the S3 API
solves these issues, as the locking mechanics are handled in the external
storage service.

As a practical matter, this involves removing the assumption of working with a
local filesystem to the EDD startup script, adding a configurable storage
backend for the `edd.load` app over simply re-using the default upload backend,
and offering an admin task to migrate from previous storage to the S3 storage.

Add show password button to login page

Having a password field always obscure the field contents can make the field
difficult to use if the user is unclear of what they have typed (e.g. has
tremors, types fast). Having the option to reveal the contents of the password
field can allow a user to review it, and correct it, without needing to submit
the form and fill out the password all over again.

This feature is behind a feature flag, and is disabled by default. There is a
trade-off between usability and security for a feature like this. Since the
LBNL deployments of EDD accept LBNL LDAP credentials to login, it is an
inappropriate accommodation to make considering the consequences of
unintentional password reveal.

Add unique task queues per task

Due to using only one default queue for all tasks, we experience big
performance issues in EDD when that queue gets flooded with tasks that take a
long time. A particular problem appears when several tasks to check UniProt are
in the queue, since the task is rate-limited. With only one queue, if several
of these are in line, nothing else can execute until the backlog is cleared.

By switching to a queue per task, the worker processes can consume messages of
every task. This will let tasks execute, even if a particular queue gets filled
up and is executing slowly.

Using the `task_create_missing_queues` setting to automatically generate a
queue from names, and assigning all current task names to a queue of the same
name. The workers are already starting with only an exchange name, and should
consume messages from all the queues in the exchange.

Note: the line lengths for the task names are long, and flake8 complains about
them. If trying to break the line, black will revert it back. There may be a
better way to do this someday, but not today.

Fix user lookup when login with email

The authentication backend for LDAP would resolve either username or email to a
DN for authn, but would then always use the "login" field to resolve as a
Django username. When a user tries to authenticate with the other value in the
"login" field, LDAP continued to resolve, but Django would end up creating a
new User record, because username != email. The change here short-circuits
this, by taking advantage of the LDAP backend always creating an EmailAddress
record for LDAP logins. Now, if someone first logs in with an email, then logs
in with a username, the backend will check the EmailAddress record from the
LdapUser record first, before trying to create a duplicate account.

Fix extension issue in import React scripts

The React code for the wizard import to EDD had a small mis-configuration.
Webpack would not build the scripts without having imports retain the `.tsx`
extensions on imports. At the same time, `tsc` and `eslint` and other tools
would complain about the extension existing. So some tools would not work
unless the extension is included, and other tools would not work unless the
extension is omitted. Adding in the `.tsx` extension in the Webpack
resolve.extensions config fixes the issue.

easier use in `Dockerfile` builds.

requires running the script. Any deviations from the typical task can use the
script as a guideline.

Fix Description view for user with Read access

When viewing a Study where the logged in user only has Read level access, the
lines table in the Description view would be empty. This turned out to be
caused by the drag-n-drop element to add more Line entries with an Experiment
Setup File, which would not be added to the page for a user who could not write
new Lines. The setup code for the table would still try to setup the dropzone
element, but fail when trying to index the first entry in the selector for the
dropzone. This failure then causes the rest of the table setup to not execute.
Updating the dropzone module to first check if the selector passed to the
initialization code has one (and only one) item, allows for the code to safely
skip over the missing element, and continue rendering the table.

Replace patched cleanse_setting with new API

Django prior to 3.2 used a function `django.views.debug.cleanse_setting()` to
replace any potentially sensitive parameters in settings with an obfuscated
value (a string of asterisks). In Django 3.2+, this function is replaced by a
SafeExceptionReporterFilter class, that handles cleansing settings, as well as
sensitive parameters in request META headers and post parameters, when
reporting values in errors.

EDD was using a monkey-patched version of `cleanse_setting`, that checked for
keys likely to contain URLs, then parse those URLs and replace any found
passwords with asterisks. Now that the original function is gone and refactored
into a class swappable in settings, moved the patched code into a sub-class of
the new class, and changed the base EDD settings to load our version of
the class.

Add testing-specific Redis cache configs

For some time, there has been an issue with intermittent test failures when
running EDD's tests, particularly when using a single test environment with
repeated test runs in succession (i.e. development). I had assumed that this
may be a problem with unintended cache collisions, where a randomized username

This config change adds a new file to `edd.settings`, which imports everything
from `edd.settings` and alters the `CACHES` setting to use an alternative cache
URL if it's provided. The pytest config then uses this settings file as it's
Django Settings, so the alternative URL is used for all tests. We have to do it
this way, instead of simply overriding the settings on each test, because the
`django_redis` package fixes its settings at startup time, and overriding
settings after the fact will have no effect.

Also added are two pytest fixtures, one that will run the Redis command
`BGREWRITEAOF` to re-write the append-only file after all tests in the session
are run, and the other to flush (i.e. delete everything) the cache before each
test run. This ensures that every test is guaranteed a clean cache. Both
fixtures only apply when a testing cache is configured.

Fix flickering select-all checkbox

The Handsontable library used to display tables of EDD data will frequently
redraw table headers via replacing the DOM nodes for those headers. There was a
checkbox explicitly rendered as a select-all control for the line, assay, and
measurement table views, to handle selecting or de-selecting all items shown in
the table. This worked, but the UI would show a flicker whenever the table
state changed, due to the Handsontable library frequently replacing the input
and its current state, with a new checkbox having cleared state.

This code is now refactored, so the control to toggle selection states is added
to the DOM outside of the table during table setup. Since the control is no
longer part of the headers, there's no problems with the control getting
replaced and showing a flicker in the UI. With the control existing outside of
the table, some additional code is required to position the control as if it
were in the table headers.

As an additional side effect, more of the code dealing with configuring options

Fix slow tests on notifications

Several of the notification tests were annotated with `django_db` and the
`transaction=True` argument. These tests turned out to take an excessive amount
of time with the database, taking around 16-17 seconds each on slower test VMs.
However, removing the annotation from the tests causes the tests to fail. What
appeared to be happening is that the test setup created a fake user in a
transaction, but the async code used a different database connection object to
read back the user ID that's "logged in", so the session information added as a
session cookie does not validate. The fake user ends up not existing, and all
the tests run as if for an anonymous user. The `transaction=True` argument
seems to set a savepoint, create and commit the database record, then instruct
the database to rollback to the savepoint at the end, taking a significant
amount of time.

The `pytest` configuration is now updated to report the ten slowest test calls,
setups, and teardowns. In CI, one of these should always be the test setup that
creates the test database from migrations, currently a process taking about 25
seconds. In development, this can be greatly reduced with the use of the
`--reuse-db` flag to `pytest`, with the caveat that `--create-db` must also be
used whenever any schema changes are made to the code.

Improve handling of transcriptomics type lookups

Handling types for transcriptomics is a bit different than all the other types,
as the EDD stakeholders have not settled on any "blessed" external source(s)
for names. The app supports looking up entries in the linked ICE instance as
the only supported "global" names. All others are treated as user-scoped names.
When looking up a gene name, e.g. "X-23", if the linked ICE has a part "X-23",
then that is the type. If Alice adds data for "X-23", and it's *not* in the
linked ICE, then EDD creates an "X-23" type unique to Alice. If Barbara also
adds data for "X-23", then EDD creates an "X-23" distinct from the one created
for Alice.

This behavior is also our work-around for the difficulty of adding new types to
EDD. Where the "official" way to add a type is to use the identifier from the
"blessed" external database, like PubChem; or, request an admin add the type
for you. Instead, importing data as "omics" would fall back to treating
anything unknown as a `GeneIdentifier`.

Eventually, we want all types in EDD to be mapped to canonical references in
external databases, i.e. NCBI for genes. There is a flag `provisional` on every
type record, which is meant to indicate that it's a type created in EDD without
validation from one of these external databases. However, the `GeneIdentifier`
models were not making use of the flag.

This update changes the code responsible for looking up and creating the
`GeneIdentifier` model records, to make it aware of the `provisional` flag. An
out-of-band database update will execute to bring existing records in line with
how new records will be created. The code for this update is:

```python
from main.models import GeneIdentifier
GeneIdentifier.objects.filter(strainlink__isnull=True).update(provisional=True)
```

The result of the change here will not be visible to ordinary users of EDD, nor
to web-interface-only admins of EDD. It will enable the updated import code to
better make a small change in behavior, along with its new features. As the new
import code will allow for choosing a measurement type from an autocomplete
search if none is found, there will be less need to rely on EDD to correctly
guess the type intended by users, and less need to automatically create new
types. The plan is to have the updated import not automatically create new
types during the lookup phase, and instead push the type creation to the
"Interpret" phase. This will result in fewer "bogus" types being created in the
database from failed, partial, or erroneous import files.

Add privlege drop to run_tests.sh script

EDD's normal execution uses an entrypoint script that runs as `root` for
initial setup, then `exec`s the application itself as the `edduser` account.
This can cause a clash when developing EDD, and using both the application and
running tests with the builtin `run_tests.sh` script as `root`. The test runner
would write directories to disk as `root`, and the application could try to
also write to directories owned by `root`, when the expectation is the
directory would be owned by `edduser`.

This update adds a check to `run_tests.sh`, and when it's executed by `root`,
the script will `exec` itself with `setpriv` to drop execution privleges to
`edduser` similar to how the entrypoint script drops to `edduser` with `gosu`.
The mechanism here is a little different, using `setpriv` instead of `gosu`;
the latter is specifically designed for dropping privleges in a Docker
entrypoint, and has potential issues when used from an interactive TTY (as
when `docker exec` into the container to run tests interactively).

Django username. When a user tries to authenticate with the other value in the
"login" field, LDAP continued to resolve, but Django would end up creating a
new User record, because username != email. The change here short-circuits
this, by taking advantage of the LDAP backend always creating an EmailAddress
record for LDAP logins. Now, if someone first logs in with an email, then logs
in with a username, the backend will check the EmailAddress record from the
LdapUser record first, before trying to create a duplicate account.

Add detection of logout to websockets

This has bugged me for a while. When a user has an EDD page open in a tab for a
long time, and their normal HTTP session expires, the websocket connection
stays open. This is not detectable normally, but when new versions are
deployed, the server closes old websockets. The frontend code tries to
reconnect, and fails--because the session is now invalid. That open tab will
then continue trying to reconnect, until it is closed or the user tries to
navigate elsewhere.

With this detection code added, when the reconnect attempt fails a few times,
it will kick off a "ping" request to EDD, which will fail if the current
session is invalid. If the session does turn out to be invalid, the code will
reload the page, to force the user to login again. This process has to be
outside of the websocket connection, because the protocol intentionally does
not provide any information on why connections fail.

    The decorator ends up being a complicated no-op. The idea from the decorator
    docstring is to prevent multiple calls to get_queryset() on a single request,
    with the implication being that get_queryset() results in a database query.

    queries until the QuerySet is iterated, and once the query is run, the
    QuerySet itself already caches the results.

Consolidate Django template HTML/text

The locations for the various templates used in the project could be difficult
to determine. Since EDD arranges its code in multiple "apps", and each one
could potentially include a templates folder, finding the location of a
template file referenced in the code would involve checking all of them--or
running `find . -name page.html` and picking out the correct one if multiples
are found. Bundling templates this way is more important for re-usable "apps",
and none of our current code is written to be used that way. These are only for
EDD use.

This update consolidates all of our customized templates into a high-level
templates directory. Inside are all the templates for our internal apps, and
the override templates for other apps (e.g. `account` for the `django-allauth`
library app). This prevents any potential confusion about where templates
should go. They all go to the templates folder. It also eliminates problems
where a template could potentially exist in multiple locations.

Fix autofocus on search field with autocompletes

There is an unintended interaction between JQuery's handling of focus events
and the way Select2 works, where with specific versions of each library, the
search field part of an autocomplete will fail to focus. To work around the
problem, we can hook into the event where an autocomplete is opened, and use
that to trigger a native browser API focus event, skipping over JQuery's
handling of events.

Presumably, the libraries will update to fix this problem eventually. The
additional event handler and the forceFocus function should be removed once the
fix is merged upstream.

See: https://github.com/select2/select2/issues/5993

The tests for notifications started having some issues with timeouts after the
last downtime patching. One of the symptoms is having an async test fail with
the default timeout of one second, which then causes all subsequent tests to
fail as the event loop used for the first connection is reset. The errors in
the tests would look like this:

FAILED tests.py::test_A - AssertionError: Exceeded websocket timeout
FAILED tests.py::test_B - RuntimeError: <asyncio.locks.Lock object at 0x7f20267f0a50 [locked]> is bound to a different event loop
FAILED tests.py::test_C - RuntimeError: <asyncio.locks.Lock object at 0x7f20267f0a50 [locked]> is bound to a different event loop
FAILED tests.py::test_D - RuntimeError: <asyncio.locks.Lock object at 0x7f20267f0a50 [locked]> is bound to a different event loop
FAILED tests.py::test_E - RuntimeError: <asyncio.locks.Lock object at 0x7f20267f0a50 [locked]> is bound to a different event loop

The tests are now updated such that every test gets its own event loop, and the
ASGI application for notifications is initialized with that event loop. Also
added are a few helper classes for dealing with responses on updates to
notifications, so it's a little easier to read the test code and understand
what's going on with named functions instead of a bunch of nested key lookups
on the responses.

model for them at this time; we use a hard-coded list of three possible values.

values, for the time in the future where we may have more values (or a database

REST API schema, so it updated to be a regular `ViewSet` instead of a faked
`ModelViewSet`. But, doing this removed the paging functionality that REST API
consumers in the data page are expecting. This updates the endpoint to include
a static "page" structure in the response.

Update ProteinIdentifier model to prevent race

There is a potential race condition when EDD is importing data with new-to-EDD
protein accession IDs, where background tasks can near-simultaneously attempt
to create a new protein record for a given accession. This is now prevented by
a uniqueness constraint on the accession code field, and using the atomic
`get_or_create` Django QuerySet method instead of a `get` and a `create` in the
`Model.DoesNotExist` exception handler.

The instances where this is a problem have been fixed out-of-band with the code
snippet here:

```
from django.db.models import Count
from main.models import Measurement, ProteinIdentifier
dupes = ProteinIdentifier.objects.values("accession_code").annotate(count=Count("accession_code")).filter(count__gt=1)
for p in dupes:
  first = ProteinIdentifier.objects.filter(accession_code=p.get("accession_code")).order_by("id").first()
  ProteinIdentifier.objects.filter(accession_code=p.get("accession_code")).exclude(id=first.id).delete()
```

The migration included here should fail if running against an instance with
duplicated accession codes. It should be impossible for any of these items to
have Measurement records linked, but to be safe, you may want to check this
before running the delete loop, assigning all Measurement records to the lowest
ID before deleting the non-lowest IDs:

```
for p in dupes:
  pids = ProteinIdentifier.objects.filter(accession_code=p.get("accession_code")).values_list("id", flat=True).order_by("id")
  Measurement.objects.filter(measurement_type_id__in=pids).update(measurement_type_id=pids[0])
```

Update run_tests.sh script to reuse test database

A significant amount of time in running the EDD test suite is consumed with
creating the database to use for executing tests. Django and `pytest` do this
by finding the configured database connection, creating a new database on the
same server with the database name prefixed with `test_`, then Django runs
through all the migrations for the database. Essentially, make a new empty
database and run `python manage.py migrate`. This work is skipped if the
`--reuse-db` flag is present, AND the database exists.

While it is important to periodically run through the migrations to verify they
still work, we don't need to do this *every* *time*; especially as the
execution time of these migrations accounts for roughly 20% of the total test
execution time. Structuring the change in this way is a compromise. Developers
running `pytest` directly will not get the `--reuse-db` flag by default, like
they would if this change was made in `server/pyproject.toml`. Jenkins builds
will use `run_tests.sh`, and if the build environment has a database, it will
use it. If the Jenkins environment does not have the test database, then there
is no effective change from current behavior.

Additionally, some async tests are still failing when run with the full test
suite. Setting up the run_tests.sh helper script to re-run test failures, so
that there's a chance for load-induced flakiness to be worked around.

Refactor redis cache interactions to utilities

In our refactorings of EDD's data processing code, we've moved to an
architecture of quick execution on HTTP responses, pushing almost all
computation into background workers with Celery, and mediating communication
between HTTP processing and background tasks with Redis cache keys. The
implementations of first data imports, then Experiment Description, each have
their own implementations of Redis interactions. These are similar
implementations, but with subtle differences as the code evolved to be better.

This refactor takes what we've learned from two separate implementations of
Redis communications in an upload / process / (un)resolved records workflow,
and pulls it out into a shared implementation of *only* the Redis primitive
operations. Both of the classes this is extracted from are trying to do lots of
(too many) things. Extracting this piece makes both classes much simpler, and
harmonizes implementations to contain the improvements we've learned about
since original authoring.

As a side-effect of the refactor, some issues with using Experiment Setup
failing to start the processing of uploaded files should be fixed.

Whenever a user logs in, the database record for that user gets updated with
the last login time set to the current time. When the database record updates,

Add edit_uri key to mkdocs.yml

The default MkDocs implementation assumes that all GitHub repos use "master" as
the default branch. We use "trunk" as the default branch, and the "master"
branch no longer exists. This assumption causes the link for "Edit in GitHub"
to return a 404 page, as the link goes to a branch that does not exist.

Changing the edit_uri key to explicitly use a path to edit in "trunk" fixes the
problem. See [the edit_uri docs][1], specifically the note section that says:

    For example, for a GitHub- or GitLab-hosted repository, the `edit_uri`
    would be automatically set as `edit/master/docs/` (Note the `edit` path
    and `master` branch).

    …

    To use a different URI than the default (for example a different branch),
    simply set the `edit_uri` to your desired string.

[1]: https://www.mkdocs.org/user-guide/configuration/#edit_uri

Code refactoring to allow for expansion This code is being modified for use in research involving flux measurements with open path line concentrations. The calculations have not changed much; however, the code was reorganized to reduce creep and make the code more modular. More modular should make new features easier to add. Some new features have been added including: (1) Warning messages are formatted identically so it is clear the windrose function is generating the warning and it is not coming from outside the windrose function. (2) Guards have been placed to check if the incoming data is in the correct form. This may alleviate issue #103. In the original implementation, if the incoming data is formatted wrong it is hard to tell what is wrong because errors may be anything generated anywhere. (3) More warnings are included so the user knows about situations like datapoints falling outside of the ws.int and/or breaks specifications. (4) A maximum can now be specified for the interval rings. This is to prevent the graph from displaying unrealistic frequency lines greater than 100% windRose(mydata, grid.line = list(max = 100)) (5) The width of grid lines can be adjusted windRose(mydata, grid.line = list(lwd = 2)) (6) For big plots a finer circle can be made by doubling the resolution factor WindRose(mydata, grid.line = list(res = 2)) (7) An anticipated direction arrow can be added. This is useful for determining if the wind blew in an anticipated direction. windRose(mydata, grid.line = list(gridArrow = 180)) (8) The breaks are calculated differently. If nothing is given pretty values are used. If a vector is given then the vector is used. If a vector is given, but not all the points are included a warning is issued before adding a break. (9) dig.lab default was changed to 0... Not sure if this was for the best, but it is easy to change back. It may be worth it to accept input as a named list so specific variables can be controlled. Internal Changes to the code: (1) mydata is no longer treated as a mutable variable. Changes are saved in the statdata variable instead. (2) windspeed and pollution are better separated. If a variable says wind speed then it is more likely windspeed. (3) As best as possible limited the characters per line to 80 so it displays well on most screens. (4) As best as possible removed dots (.) from name to avoid confusion with the dot operator. lower camel case was used instead. (5) Avoided repetition of code as much as possible. (6) Used functions to delineate tasks such as drawing the individual elements. This should make the code much simpler to upgrade. (7) the name 'results' has been changed to 'pltData' because with results it is confusing about which results. (8) Angle360 function automatically coerces angles between (0 - 360] (9) DegtoRad performs the degrees to radians calculation (8) One computation was confusing... First the wind direction angle is set into intervals line 533 - mydata[[wd]] <- angle * ceiling(mydata[[wd]] / angle - 0.5) Then the average wind direction is calculated from angles set to intervals line 610 - ## calculate mean wd - useful for cases comparing two met data sets - u <- mean(sin(2 * pi * mydata[[wd]] / 360), na.rm = TRUE) - v <- mean(cos(2 * pi * mydata[[wd]] / 360), na.rm = TRUE) - mean.wd <- atan2(u, v) * 360 / 2 / pi The proposed version works differently averages wind direction from non-interval data. (9) The concept of an apothem is introduced to make understanding lengths in the plot simple. The apothem of a square goes from the center to the mid-point of one of the sides. In progress: (1) Plotting a point with the average wind speed and direction directly on the wind rose. This will be used as a means to determine the quality of an average wind speed and direction. This feature is already included, but the average wind speed is in the wrong spot.

* [SDS-335] Resolve import cycles using postponed annotations

Postponed annotations allow us to use forward code references without having access to them statically, but we can have access at runtime. Using the TYPE_CHECKING constant from typing makes sure that we don't have circular dependencies in the actual code.

The "correct" approach would be to extract interfaces. For example, we could have a generic API interface or a generic Job interface that exposes the methods and properties that we need access to. However, this is not particularly "Pythonese", so this approach seemed more lightweight.

[SDS-335] Resolve import cycles using postponed annotations

Postponed annotations allow us to use forward code references without having access to them statically, but we can have access at runtime. Using the TYPE_CHECKING constant from typing makes sure that we don't have circular dependencies in the actual code.

The "correct" approach would be to extract interfaces. For example, we could have a generic API interface or a generic Job interface that exposes the methods and properties that we need access to. However, this is not particularly "Pythonese", so this approach seemed more lightweight.

Add support for tracking intermittently disappearing points

We have to add the concept of live and not live points for this to work.
Each object has its own life cycle, but internally each point in an
object will now have its own life cycle as well to be able to know which
points from each object are currently being detected and tracked and
which aren't.

In the past we only tracked points which would not dissapear. Which
required us to be careful with filtering detections before feeding them
into the tracker, now this is not a problem anymore. We can just feed
any noisy detection into the tracker and track all the points in it.

Had to modify R to make the velocities on the process model less certain
as it was creating problems for detectors that return (0, 0) for
not detected points. When these points finally get their first real
detection, the tracker sees a huge velocity for the point to have moved
from (0, 0) to wherever they went, and this velocity is then slow to
correct as the following velocity vectors will be much smaller that this
first one. Reducing the velocity certainty in the process model
mitigates this, though I want to futher improve this still in the
future.

Add support for tracking intermittently disappearing points

We have to add the concept of live and not live points for this to work.
Each object has its own life cycle, but internally each point in an
object will now have its own life cycle as well to be able to know which
points from each object are currently being detected and tracked and
which aren't.

In the past we only tracked points which would not dissapear. Which
required us to be careful with filtering detections before feeding them
into the tracker, now this is not a problem anymore. We can just feed
any noisy detection into the tracker and track all the points in it.

Had to modify R to make the velocities on the process model less certain
as it was creating problems for detectors that return (0, 0) for
not detected points. When these points finally get their first real
detection, the tracker sees a huge velocity for the point to have moved
from (0, 0) to wherever they went, and this velocity is then slow to
correct as the following velocity vectors will be much smaller that this
first one. Reducing the velocity certainty in the process model
mitigates this, though I want to futher improve this still in the
future.

Separate object updates in two stages, initialized and not initialized

We had some cases in which two detections would be close to each other,
and one of them would update an already established tracked object and
the other, left unmatched, would create a new tracked objects.

Then one of those detections would dissapear and the remaining detection
could be assigned to the not yet initialized tracked object instead of
the initialized one, effectively killing the initialized object, with
the not yet initialized one taking its place.

This is not ideal as it would split what should've been a single object
into two objects, creating an unnecessary id change, which is
effectively an error in tracking.

By separating tracking in two stages, and giving initialized objects
first bids this problem is avoided.

Change the algorithm we use to match detections with tracked objects

We used to do our matches so that they would minimize the global
detection-object distance, but found that sometimes this sacrificed
an obvious match with very low distance, for erroneous matches with
higher distance each but which resulted in a lower total distance,
and this created errors in matching.

In order not to leave a detection unmatched the algorithm would
rearrange matches, sacrificing obviously correct matches as this would
allocate matches for more object-detecion pairs and this would minimize
the global distance.

An example of an errenous match caused by this can be seen in the video
"/mnt/hdd1/lalo/videos/in/cu.mp4" @ 1:52 minutes.

Match subnets in O(n^3) via linear_sum_assignment.

To solve subnets, instead of brute-forcing the n! combinations, use
scipy.optimize.linear_sum_assignment (commonly known as the
Hungarian/Munkres algorithm, although scipy actually uses a different
algorithm) which provides a solution in O(n^3).  This is not an original
idea; see e.g.
https://imagej.net/imagej-wiki-static/TrackMate_Algorithms.html#Solving_LAP

Locally, this method solves the "slow" example in adaptive-search.ipynb
(`tracks_regular = trackpy.link_df(cg, 0.75)`) in ~50ms instead of 1min.
linear_sum_assignment ("lsa") was extensively benchmarked in scipy
PR#12541 (which was most about adding a *sparse* variant, but one can
just look at the performance of lsa), which shows sub-second runtimes
for thousands of inputs.  This is also why this PR fully skips the use
of MAX_SUB_NET (at most, one may consider setting an alternate value in
the thousands for this strategy...).

The docs will need to be updated, but this PR is just to discuss the
implementation.

Use versioneer to handle version numbers

versioneer (https://github.com/warner/python-versioneer) automatically
creates version strings based on git tags and the latest commit hash.
To create a new version, simply `git tag` and versioneer will update
everything when setup.py is called. When not working from a release (for
development), trackpy.__version__ will have:

* the last version
* the number of commits since the last version
* the latest commit hash
* 'dirty' if the repo has uncommitted modifications

e.g., `0.2.1-8-g608fc6e-dirty` for this specific commit.

This allows better provenance tracking since most research work is
probably done from `master` anyway.

Fixing rolling sum calculations to use Pandas API correctly.

This fixes an issue with how the rolling sum calculations were implemented.

The pre-0.18 pandas rolling sum calculation called the Pandas API
incorrectly:
* Version 0.13.0 implements the [`rolling_mean()`](http://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/version/0.13/generated/pandas.rolling_mean.html?highlight=rolling#pandas.rolling_mean)
        function from the module level, as in, `pd.rolling_mean(my_df)`, while the `_pandas_rolling_pre_018()`
        method in utils implements it as `df.rolling_mean()`. This
        commit fixes that incorrect API implementation.

The post-0.18 pandas rolling sum calculation did not use the Pandas API
correctly:
* Version 0.18.1, released in May 2016, did away with `pd.rolling_mean(df)`
        and updated it with `df.rolling().mean()`. See the [Version 0.18.1 What's New page](http://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/version/0.18/whatsnew.html?highlight=rolling_mean)
        for the update. This was implemented incorrectly because trackpy
        only called `df.rolling()`, which returns a Rolling object. The
        Rolling object does not have a cumulative sum `cumsum()`
        function, which caused an exception to be thrown from the
        `compute_drift()` function when `cumsum()` was called on the
        Rolling object.

To do:
* We still need to add a test for the `compute_drift()` function that
        uses a rolling sum parameter. However, there are additional
        issues with the tests (namely, conflicts with old Pandas
        versions) that will require a separate pull request to update
        the tests.

This pull request will not implement a test of the `compute_drift()`
function. Rather, updates to tests will be implemented as a separate PR.

Fix rolling sum parameter in compute_drift.

This fixes an issue with how the rolling sum parameter was being used.

The issue:
The pandas rolling() function returns a Rolling object, which does not
have a cumulative sum function cumsum(). The cumsum() function is called
on the trajectory dataframe, which works fine if no rolling sum
parameter is passed, but if there is a rolling sum parameter passed,
the cumsum() function is being called on a Rolling object, which is
undefined, causing compute_drift() to crash with an exception
(Rolling object does not have a cumsum() function).

The fix:
This fixes the problem by calling sum() on the Rolling object,
which returns a dataframe. The cumsum() function can now be called
on the function.

To do:
Add a test for compute_drift() that uses a rolling sum parameter.
This problem would have been caught with more comprehensive test
coverage.

ENH Anisotropic feature characterization

A number of changes that reach deep into the feature finding: please
review carefully! The fixes are linked in subtle ways, that's why this
is one big commit.

- Changes the behaviour of the `mass` column: it is now calculated from
the raw image. This solves the issue #237 due to the rescaling of the
processed image and the subsequent calculation of mass on this image.
- Changes the behaviour of the `signal` column: previously it was
calculated from the raw image and subsequently the `black_level` was
subtracted. Because of the high sensitivity to noise, this gives
unpredictable results. It has been changed to: `signal =
preprocessed_feature.max()`. The rescaling has been accounted for via an
extra variable coming from `scale_to_gamut`.
- eccentricity is calculated on anisotropic masks too, assuming that
pixels are square
- size is calculated in all directions separately when an anisotropic
mask is used, giving `size_x`, `size_y` columns
- filtering on `maxsize` is done on sqrt(size_x**2 + size_y**2), which
equals the current behaviour if sizes are equal
- static error is calculated in all directions separately when an
anisotropic mask is used *or* when noise_size is anisotropic, giving
`ep_x`, `ep_y` columns
- `preprocessing.bandpass` now calculates the background level and
standard deviation (only if needed, defaults to current behaviour)
- `scale_to_gamut` returns the scale factor (only if needed, defaults to
current behaviour)
- docstring for eccentricity: 0 is circular, not 1 as it is documented
now
- characterization arrays are only initialized if needed

FIX Gaps in frames are not ignored anymore

Don't sort links before applying them.

This should not have any effects on the linking(?) given that the
sorting is by x/y coordinate, which is basically arbitrary.

This speeds up the simple example below by ~15%
```python
import time
import numpy as np
from pandas import DataFrame
import trackpy as tp; tp.ignore_logging()

n_particles = 50
n_frames = 10000
frame_size = 200
starting = np.random.random((n_particles, 2)) * frame_size
dxys = np.random.standard_normal((n_frames, n_particles, 2))
xys = starting + np.cumsum(dxys, axis=0)
frames = []
xs = []
ys = []
for f in range(n_frames):
    for p in range(n_particles):
        if np.random.random() < 0.5:  # Kill half of the localizations.
            continue
        frames.append(f)
        xs.append(xys[f, p, 0])
        ys.append(xys[f, p, 1])
df = DataFrame({"frame": frames, "x": xs, "y": ys})

__start = time.perf_counter()
tp.link_df(df, 3, memory=10)
print("elapsed", time.perf_counter() - __start)
```

On personal datasets the speedup goes up to 2x(!).

Use versioneer to handle version numbers

versioneer (https://github.com/warner/python-versioneer) automatically
creates version strings based on git tags and the latest commit hash.
To create a new version, simply `git tag` and versioneer will update
everything when setup.py is called. When not working from a release (for
development), trackpy.__version__ will have:

* the last version
* the number of commits since the last version
* the latest commit hash
* 'dirty' if the repo has uncommitted modifications

e.g., `0.2.1-8-g608fc6e-dirty` for this specific commit.

This allows better provenance tracking since most research work is
probably done from `master` anyway.
